title: Wine law and labels
lead: How the big wine countries rank and protect their wines, the US labeling percentages, and how to read what a label is telling you.

intro.title: TWO EU TIERS, MANY NAMES
intro.text: In Europe, protected wine sits in two EU tiers. Each country uses its own words for them.

tiers.name: PDO / DOP / AOP
tiers.note: France AOC/AOP, Italy DOCG and DOC, Spain DO and DOCa, Germany Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein

tiers.name: PGI / IGP
tiers.note: France IGP, Italy IGT, Spain Vino de la Tierra

sections.name: Old World, New World

lines.label: Three label styles
lines.text: Wines are labeled by grape, by region, or by a made-up name. Old World countries mostly label by region. The region's law decides which grapes go in.

lines.label: What the terms mean
lines.text: Old World means the countries where modern winemaking traditions began, like France and Italy. New World means countries that borrowed them, like the US, Australia and Chile.

know: A Chablis label says Chablis, not Chardonnay.
Made-up names are often blends that break a region's rules, like the first Super Tuscans.
Old World style tends to be lighter, lower in alcohol and higher in acid; this is typical, not a rule.
The exam asks you to read grape, color and style from a label.

visuals.title: Three ways a wine is labeled

items.name: By name
items.text: A made-up name, often a blend

sections.name: France: AOC, AOP and IGP

lines.label: AOP
lines.text: Every production step happens in one defined area, by known methods. The rules sit in a 'cahier des charges' approved by the EU.

lines.label: AOC and IGP
lines.text: AOC is the national step before EU registration as AOP; wines may still print AOC. IGP links a wine to its origin; for wine, harvest to finished wine happens in the zone.

know: AOP is the EU sign; AOC is the French national equivalent.
Only wine may keep using the term AOC.
INAO has run France's origin system since 1935.
IGP wines are also checked by state-certified bodies.
Southern Rhône tiers: Côtes du Rhône, Côtes du Rhône Villages, then single-village crus like Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
In Alsace, a grape named on the label means 100% of that grape.

items.title: Protected origin
items.text:
All steps in one area
Known local know-how
EU-approved rules

items.label: IGP
items.title: Geographic indication
items.text:

sections.name: Italy: DOCG, DOC and IGT

lines.label: The tiers
lines.text: Italy splits its DOP wines into DOCG and DOC. IGT is Italy's word for IGP. A DOCG must have been a DOC for at least seven years.

lines.label: Label words
lines.text: Classico means the oldest zone. Riserva means extra aging. Superiore means lower yields and more alcohol.

know: DOCG rules must be stricter than the DOC they came from.
Riserva: at least two years for reds, one year for whites.
Gran Selezione is only for DOCG wines from the estate's own grapes.
DO wines must show a vintage, except fortified, non-vintage sparkling and frizzante.
The Court also lists Secco, Amabile, Charmat and Appassimento as Veneto label words; they are taught in the Italy chapter.

sections.name: Spain: DO, DOCa and Pago

lines.label: The tiers
lines.text: Vino de la Tierra is Spain's IGP. DO needs prestige and five years as a quality region. DOCa needs ten years as a DO and bottling inside the zone.

lines.label: Aging words
lines.text: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva climb in minimum aging. Level 1 needs the order, not the exact times.

know: Rioja is a DOCa.
Vino de Pago is a DOP from one site with its own soil and microclimate.
Under Spanish law, red Crianza needs 24 months, 6 in oak.
Rioja's own rules are longer: Crianza 2 years with 1 in oak.
Cava is a DO for traditional-method sparkling wine; Priorat is a DOCa.

rows.name: DOCa
rows.note: 10+ years as DO, bottled in zone

items.name: Reserva
items.text: 3 years, 1 in oak, 6 months in bottle

sections.name: Germany: the Prädikat levels

lines.label: The tiers
lines.text: Deutscher Wein has no named origin. Landwein is regional. Qualitätswein comes from one of 13 regions. Prädikatswein is Qualitätswein graded by ripeness at harvest.

lines.label: Ripeness, not sweetness
lines.text: Riper grapes earn a higher Prädikat. The winemaker still decides how sweet the wine ends up, so Kabinett and Spätlese can be dry.

know: Prädikatswein may not be chaptalized.
Eiswein: as ripe as Beerenauslese, picked frozen at minus 7°C or colder.
The 1971 law made ripeness at harvest the main quality measure.
Grosses Gewächs is a dry single-vineyard top wine (a VDP term, now also in the 2021 law).

visuals.title: The six Prädikate, least to most ripe

sections.name: Austria and Portugal

lines.label: Austria
lines.text: Austria's tiers run Wein, Landwein, Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein. DAC is its quality appellation, like an AOC, with set grapes and mostly dry styles.

lines.label: Portugal
lines.text: Portugal calls its protected wines DOP. Know four: Vinho Verde, Douro, Porto and Madeira.

know: DAC (Districtus Austriae Controllatus) is like an AOC or DOC: set grapes and styles, mostly dry wines.
Prädikatswein exists in Austria too, but it is rarely made; Landwein is rarely exported.
The Wachau has its own ripeness ladder; Smaragd is the ripest level.
A red-white-red band on the capsule marks Austrian quality wine.
Portugal's DOPs to know: Vinho Verde, Douro, Porto, Madeira.

rows.name: Prädikatswein
rows.note: graded by ripeness, rare in Austria

rows.name: Qualitätswein · DAC
rows.note: DAC: set grapes and styles, mostly dry

sections.name: United States: AVAs and percentages

lines.label: AVA
lines.text: An American Viticultural Area is a defined growing region with a name, its own features and a set boundary.

lines.label: The numbers
lines.text: Name a grape: 75%. Name a state or county: 75%. Name an AVA: 85%. Name a vineyard: 95%. A vintage with an AVA: 95%.

know: A vintage with a state or county appellation needs 85%; with an AVA, 95%.
'Estate bottled' needs an AVA and grapes grown on the winery's own or controlled land.
Naming two or more grapes means listing each percentage.
Showing a vintage or grape name means the label must show an appellation.
The Court lists Oregon at 90% for most varietals and 95% for AVAs.

visuals.title: US federal minimums
visuals.note: TTB rules, 27 CFR part 4. Vintage with a non-AVA appellation: 85%.

sections.name: New World origin rules

lines.label: Origin only
lines.text: A Chilean DO or an Australian GI names where the grapes grew. It adds no other rules, unlike a European appellation.

lines.label: The percentages
lines.text: Argentina, Australia and New Zealand need 85% of a named grape. South Africa needs 100% from a single named appellation.

know: Chile's DO levels, big to small: Region, Subregion, Zone, Area.
South Africa's Wine of Origin levels, big to small: Geographical Unit, Region, District, Ward.
Australia's GIs, big to small: Australia, State, Zone, Region, Sub-Region.
South Eastern Australia is a huge zone used for high-volume wine.
Canada has no national wine law; each province sets its own, and VQA oversees premium wine.
The Court's guide says Mexico has no wine laws.

visuals.title: Named-grape minimums
visuals.note: Court guide figures. South Africa: 100% from a single named appellation.

visuals.title: Big to small: three ways to nest a place

sections.name: Reading a label

lines.label: Five parts
lines.text: Producer, region, grape or appellation, vintage, and alcohol. If no grape is named, the appellation's rules tell you what's inside.

lines.label: Watch for
lines.text: Estate bottling has its own phrase in each language. 'Reserve' and 'Old Vines' have no official meaning in many places.

know: Chablis = Chardonnay, Chianti = Sangiovese, even though the label won't say so.
NV means non-vintage, a blend of years.
Mis en bouteille au château/domaine is French for estate bottled.
Imbottigliato all'origine is the Italian equivalent.
Burgundy label words: Négociant, Domaine, Clos (walled vineyard), Monopole (one owner), Vieilles Vignes (old vines).

visuals.title: What to find on any label

mixups.why: AOP is the EU-wide protection; AOC is France's national step before it, still allowed on wine labels.
DOCG sits above DOC, needs 7+ years as a DOC and stricter rules.
DOCa needs 10+ years as a DO and bottling inside the zone; Rioja and Priorat are DOCa.
85% of the grapes must come from the AVA; 95% must come from the stated year.

sources: INAO, Italian Law 238/2016, Spain's Ley 6/2015 (BOE), Consejo Regulador DOCa Rioja, Wines of Germany (DWI), TTB and 27 CFR part 4 (eCFR), and the Court of Master Sommeliers Americas curriculum guide, with Wine Folly as a labelled secondary source. Checked Oct 31, 2026; aligned with the Court’s Introductory curriculum Nov 2, 2026, adding the Court guide’s Austria, Portugal and New World law rows, Wine Australia’s GI register, Der Standard (Austrian banderole) and the Wine Spectator glossary.

facts.fact: Introductory exam content: wine law of important regions (connecting grapes with places or appellations, and appellations with styles) and reading a wine label (determining grape variety, color and style from the label).
Section 3 of the Introductory course outline is 'Understanding Wine Law'.
Regional wine laws dictate which grape varieties can be grown and how they are grown in many wine regions.
Wines are labeled in one of three ways: by grape variety, by region, or by a made-up name.
Labeling by region is used mostly in Old World countries such as France, Italy, Spain and Portugal; each region dictates which grapes may be used (e.g. Chablis is Chardonnay, Chianti is Sangiovese).
Named (made-up) wines are often blends that don't fit a region's wine law; Tuscan wines with French grapes such as Merlot, Syrah and Cabernet gave rise to the first Super Tuscans.
Wine Folly's varietal minimums: 75% USA (Oregon 90%), 80% Argentina, 85% for Italy, France, Germany, Austria, Portugal, New Zealand, South Africa, Australia and the UK.

'Old World' refers to traditional winemaking countries such as France, Italy, Spain, Portugal and Germany; 'New World' refers to countries that borrowed those traditions, e.g. North and South America, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand.

Old World wine tends to have lighter body, lower alcohol, higher acidity and less fruit; New World wine tends toward fuller body, higher alcohol, lower acidity and pronounced fruit. These are typical, not rules.

Five basic parts of a label: producer or name, region, variety or appellation, vintage or non-vintage (NV), alcohol by volume. NV wines can pull wine from multiple vintages. 'Old Vines' has no rule for how old the vines must be.
A Chablis label does not mention Chardonnay; an appellation wine relies on the appellation's rules to tell you what's in the bottle.
Estate-bottled terms: Mis en bouteille au château / au domaine (France), Imbottigliato all'origine (Italy), Erzeugerabfüllung (Germany).
'Reserve' on a label has no official meaning (Wine Folly); the Court's guide says 'Reserve has no legal meaning' for California.

AOP (Appellation d'origine protégée) is a product whose production steps are all carried out according to recognized know-how in one geographic area. It is a European sign that protects the name across the EU.
AOC (appellation d'origine contrôlée) is the mandatory national recognition step before a name is registered as an AOP. Only wine products keep the right to use the AOC term if they wish.
AOP rules are written in a cahier des charges defined by producers and approved by the EU, and checked by an independent body approved by INAO.

IGP identifies a product whose quality, reputation or other traits are linked to its geographic origin. At least one step of production must happen in the area; for wine, every operation from grape harvest to the end of winemaking happens in the zone.
INAO has been at the heart of French origin policy since 1935.
Italian law 238/2016, art. 28: DOP wines are classified as DOCG and DOC; IGP wines use the Italian term IGT. The Italian and EU terms may appear alone or together on the label.

Art. 33: DOCG is reserved for wines already DOC for at least seven years, judged of particular merit; DOC is reserved for wines from zones recognized as IGT for at least five years. A DOCG must have stricter rules than its DOC.
Art. 31: 'Classico' is for the oldest zone of origin (e.g. Chianti Classico). 'Riserva' needs at least two years of aging for reds and one year for whites.
Art. 31: 'Superiore' needs at least 10% lower yield per hectare and at least 0.5% more alcohol than the base wine. 'Gran Selezione' is only for DOCG wines made from the bottling estate's own grapes.
Art. 31: DO wines must show the vintage on the label, except fortified (liquorosi), non-vintage sparkling and frizzante wines.
Court guide for Piedmont lists the classification as IGP, DOC, DOCG, and label terms Normale and Riserva.
Spain (Ley 6/2015): 'Vino de la Tierra' marks an IGP wine; 'Vino de calidad de' marks a DOP wine.
'Denominación de origen' needs high commercial prestige and a region recognized as a quality wine with geographical indication for at least five years.
'Denominación de origen calificada' needs, on top of DO rules, at least 10 years using the term DO, and sale only in bottle from registered wineries inside the zone.
'Vino de pago' is a DOP from a 'pago': a rural site with its own soil and microclimate, known by a name tied to vine growing. All grapes must come from vineyards in the pago.

National aging terms for red DOP wines: Crianza at least 24 months with at least 6 in oak barrels of up to 330 liters; Reserva 36 months with at least 12 in oak; Gran Reserva 60 months with at least 18 in oak.

Rioja red: Crianza at least two years with at least one year in 225-liter oak barrels; Reserva at least three years with at least one in oak and six months in bottle; Gran Reserva at least five years with two in oak and two in bottle.
Court guide: Rioja is a DOCa. Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva are aging tiers in ascending order of minimum time; knowing the actual times is not necessary at the Introductory level.

Court guide, Germany: wine without geographic indication is Deutscher Wein; with GI: Landwein (regional), Qualitätswein (from one of the 13 Anbaugebiete) and Prädikatswein (a subset of Qualitätswein graded by ripeness at harvest). Chaptalization is not allowed for Prädikatswein.

The six Prädikate in order of ripeness: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein (same ripeness level as Beerenauslese), Trockenbeerenauslese. Kabinett and Spätlese are off-dry in style and can be made trocken; Beerenauslese and TBA are very sweet.
Ripeness at harvest sets the Prädikat, but choices in the winery decide how sweet the finished wine is.

VDP is a German producers' association with its own Burgundy-style vineyard classification. Grosses Gewächs: single-vineyard grand cru wines; Erstes Gewächs: premier cru. Label terms: Trocken = dry, Halbtrocken = half-dry.
The 1971 German Wine Law made ripeness at harvest the main measure of quality.
Eiswein is made from grapes as ripe as BA, harvested at minus 7°C or colder and pressed while frozen. Prädikat wines may not be enriched (chaptalized); Qualitätswein may.
Prädikatswein and Qualitätswein must come 100% from one of the 13 German growing regions and pass the quality test.
Since 1971 every Qualität and Prädikat wine has been lab-tested and sensory-tested and gets an official approval number shown on the label.

From 2021 Germany has an origin pyramid for Qualität and Prädikat wines, 'the smaller the origin, the higher the quality': single-vineyard wines (Großes Gewächs, Erstes Gewächs, other sites) at the top, then village wines (Ortswein), region wines, then the wine-growing area.
Under the 2021 rules, the term Qualitätswein can be replaced on all Qualität and Prädikat wines by 'wine with a protected designation of origin' plus the region name.
Großes Gewächs must be dry (trocken), hand-harvested, from a single vineyard, with the vintage on the label.
An American viticultural area (AVA) is a defined grape-growing region with a name, distinguishing features and a delineated boundary set in 27 CFR part 9.
US appellation rules: at least 75% from the named country, state or county; at least 85% from grapes grown in a named viticultural area. Imported wines follow the same 75% and 85% thresholds.
An appellation is required on the label when the wine shows a vintage date, a varietal name, a semi-generic name, 'estate bottled' and some other designations.

A single grape variety may be named if at least 75% of the wine is that variety, all grown in the labeled appellation. Vitis labrusca varieties may use 51% with a 'contains not less than 51%' statement.
Two or more varieties may be named only if all the grapes are those varieties and each percentage is shown on the label.
A wine may use a viticultural area name if at least 85% comes from grapes grown inside the AVA and, for US wine, it is fully finished in the state where the AVA lies.
Vintage: with an AVA appellation at least 95% of the wine must come from grapes harvested that year; with any other appellation, at least 85%.
'Estate bottled' requires an AVA appellation; the winery must be in the AVA, grow all the grapes on land it owns or controls there, and crush, ferment, age and bottle in a continuous process.
A vineyard, orchard, farm or ranch name may not appear unless 95% of the wine comes from that named place.

Court guide, California: 75% minimum grape variety, 85% minimum for AVA, 95% minimum for vintage, 95% for single vineyard, 100% for estate bottling. Reserve has no legal meaning; Meritage is a trademark.
Court guide, Catalonia: Priorat is a DOCa; Cava is a DO.
Court guide, Oregon: 90% minimum for stated variety (with exceptions such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot) and 95% minimum for AVA.
CMS curriculum guide, Winemaking (Intro) packaging: labels and label design, capsule colors and design, adhering to governmental label laws.
CMS curriculum guide, Bordeaux (Intro): Regional appellation (Bordeaux AOC), sub-regional appellations (Médoc AOP, Haut-Médoc AOP) and commune appellations (Margaux, Pauillac, St-Estèphe, St-Julien).

CMS curriculum guide, Burgundy (Intro): Regional AOP / Villages AOP / Premier Cru AOP / Grand Cru AOP. Regional AOP: Bourgogne AOP; villages such as Gevrey-Chambertin; recognize the Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos.
CMS curriculum guide, Burgundy (Intro) label terms: Négociant, Domaine, Clos, Monopole, Vieilles Vignes.

CMS curriculum guide, Southern Rhône (Intro) classification tiers: Côtes-du-Rhône AOP, Côtes-du-Rhône Villages AOP (named villages), Crus/single village (e.g. Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Tavel, Gigondas, Vacqueyras).
CMS curriculum guide, Alsace (Intro) wine law: must be 100% of the grape variety if the name is mentioned on the label.
Clos: a French term for a walled vineyard, such as Clos de Vougeot in Burgundy.
Monopole: an appellation or other designated winegrowing area controlled entirely by one winery, e.g. Domaine de la Romanée-Conti's Romanée-Conti and La Tâche.
Négociant-Manipulant (NM): a house that buys grapes or wine; all the big Champagne houses are NM.
CMS curriculum guide, Northeast Italy (Intro) general terms: Classico, Superiore, Secco, Amabile, Charmat, Appassimento.
CMS curriculum guide, Catalonia (Intro): Cava DO is traditional method sparkling, white and rosado; Priorat DOCa is mainly still, dry reds from Garnacha, Cariñena and international varieties.

CMS curriculum guide, Portugal (Intro) DOPs: Vinho Verde DOP, Douro DOP, Porto DOP, Madeira DOP. Styles: Vinho Verde low alcohol, slight effervescence; Douro bold, dry reds; Porto fortified, sweet red; Madeira fortified dry, medium dry and sweet whites.

CMS curriculum guide, Austria (Intro) wine law: without geographical indication - Wein; with GI - Landwein (regional wines, rarely exported); Qualitätswein; DAC (Districtus Austriae Controllatus): quality wine/appellation of origin, similar to the AOC or DOC system, specific grape varieties and styles permitted, focus on dry wines; Prädikatswein: like Germany but rarely produced in Austria.

CMS curriculum guide, Austria (Intro): the Wachau has its own classification system based on grape ripeness at harvest; example Smaragd, the highest level of ripeness, named for green lizards in the vineyards.

CMS curriculum guide, Austria (Intro) label terms: recognize an Austrian wine capsule (shown red-white-red). The Certified column names it the Banderole, the capsule showing the wine is Qualitätswein level or higher.
Every Austrian DAC bottle carries the red-white-red Qualitätswein banderole on its closure. (Translated from German.)
CMS curriculum guide, Canada (Intro): Canada has no national wine law; each province has its own laws. VQA (Vintners Quality Alliance) is the primary regulatory body for premium wine.
CMS curriculum guide, Mexico wine law row: 'No laws!'
CMS curriculum guide, Chile (Intro): the Denominación de Origen (DO) system refers to a geographic place of origin only, with no other additional laws. Levels: Region, Subregion, Zone, Area.
CMS curriculum guide, Argentina (Intro): 85% minimum to list the grape variety on a label.

CMS curriculum guide, South Africa (Intro): Wine of Origin system - a wine from a single appellation must be 100% from that appellation; rigorous certification. From largest area to smallest: Geographical Unit, Region, District, Ward.
CMS curriculum guide, New Zealand (Intro): Geographical Indications (GIs) are 'trademark only with no minimums, no rules'; 85% minimum to list the grape variety on a label.
CMS curriculum guide, Australia (Intro): a GI refers to a geographic place of origin only, no other additional laws; 85% labeling required for grape variety, vintage and origin.
CMS curriculum guide, Australia (Intro): GIs nest Australia, State, Zone, Region, Sub-Region, more specific as the area gets smaller; South Eastern Australia is a high-volume super GI.
The zone South Eastern Australia covers the whole of New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania and part of Queensland and South Australia.

unverified: EU varietal and vintage minimums (Wine Folly gives 85% for France, Italy, Germany and others): the EU regulation (2019/33, art. 50) could not be fetched, so no European percentage is stated as fact.

Vin de France (France's wine without geographic indication) and Italy's equivalent tier were not confirmed on an official page fetched, so the intro band only lists Germany's Deutscher Wein for that tier.
Court guide says '95% minimum for vintage' for California without the federal split; TTB rule (27 CFR 4.27) is 95% only with an AVA and 85% with other appellations. The chapter follows TTB.
Court guide says '100% for Estate Bottling; must be in the same county'. The federal rule fetched (27 CFR 4.26) ties estate bottling to an AVA, not a county; the county wording was not confirmed.
Oregon's 90%/95% rules come from the Court guide and Wine Folly only; Oregon's own regulations were not fetched.
German minimum must weights conflict between Wines of Germany pages (one says Eiswein and BA need 120°Oe; another gives 110–128°Oe by region), so no Oechsle figures are used.
The 2021 German origin pyramid allowed a transition for older labeling through the 2025 harvest; how labels look from the 2026 vintage was not checked.
The Italian law text used is the Lazio agency (ARSIAL) copy of Law 238/2016 as published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale (Vigente al 12-1-2017); later amendments were not checked.
Germany's Landwein is listed by the Court as a wine 'with geographic indication', but no official page fetched confirms it as the EU PGI tier, so it is left out of the PGI row.
Argentina's varietal minimum: the Court guide gives 85%; Wine Folly's table (fact above) gives 80%. The chapter follows the Court; Argentina's INV rules were not fetched.

New World rules (Chile, Argentina, South Africa, New Zealand, Australia, Canada, Mexico) come from the Court guide only; the official bodies' pages (Wine Australia's LIP, WOSA/SAWIS, NZ Winegrowers, Wines of Chile, VQA) were not fetched or did not load, except Wine Australia's GI register for South Eastern Australia.
Mexico 'no laws': the Court's wording. Whether Mexico has any national labeling or origin rules for wine was not checked.

New Zealand GIs as 'trademark only with no minimums, no rules' is the Court's wording; the Certified column itself says Marlborough labeling needs 100% fruit from the region, and NZ's own rules were not fetched, so the chapter only says a GI names the origin.

Austria: austrianwine.com returned 403, so Austrian tiers, DAC and the Wachau system come from the Court guide; the red-white-red banderole is also confirmed by Der Standard (in German). Whether Smaragd sits within the DAC rules today was not checked.
Burgundy label words Négociant and Domaine: listed by the Court; the négociant definition uses champagne.fr's NM definition; Domaine is not defined.

court.outcome: Germany: After studying this section, a student will understand Germany's climate, the importance of rivers, soil types, grape varieties, and learn about selected wine regions. Students will recognize the hierarchy of German wine law (Wein, Qualitätswein, Prädikatswein), and the progression of Prädikat levels. Rioja: After studying this section, a student will know the general location, climate, grape varieties, styles, and label language of Rioja. Northeast Italy: After studying this section, a student will know the major DOC/DOCGs in Northeast Italy, be able to match grape varieties with their regions, and understand general labeling terms. California Central Coast: After studying this section, a student will know selected counties of the Central Coast of California and the major AVAs within them. Students will know basic wine labeling laws and understand the relationship of climate to the grape varieties grown. Pacific Northwest: After studying this section, a student will understand the general climate, grapes grown, wine law, and AVAs of the Columbia Valley of Washington and the Willamette Valley of Oregon.

read.bigIdea: A label names a grape, a place or a made-up name.
read.where: **Old World** means the countries where winemaking traditions began, like France, Italy, Spain, Portugal and Germany. **New World** means the countries that borrowed them, like the Americas, Australia and South Africa. Old World wines tend to be lighter, lower in alcohol and higher in acid. That’s typical, not a rule.
read.stopsTitle: Three ways to label a wine

stops.name: By grape
stops.text: The label names the grape. In the US, a named grape must be at least **75%** of the wine.

stops.name: By region
stops.text: The label names the place, and the region’s law decides the grapes. **Chablis** is Chardonnay and **Chianti** is Sangiovese, but neither label says so.

stops.name: By a made-up name
stops.text: The winery invents a name. These are often blends that don’t fit a region’s rules, like the first **Super Tuscans**.

read.visualIntro: The three label styles at a glance:

keyPoints.line: is the EU sign: every step happens in one area.
is France’s national step before AOP; wine may still use it.
ties a wine to its origin: harvest to finished wine in the zone.
has led French origin policy since 1935.

read.bigIdea: In France, the place on the label is protected by law.
read.where: French protected wine uses two EU terms, **AOP** and **IGP**. AOP is the stricter one: every production step happens in one area. The body behind it all, **INAO**, has been at the heart of French origin policy since **1935**.
read.stopsTitle: Three terms on a French label

stops.name: AOP
stops.text: **Appellation d’origine protégée.** Every production step happens in one defined area, by known local methods. The rules sit in a **cahier des charges** approved by the EU.

stops.name: AOC
stops.text: **Appellation d’origine contrôlée** is France’s national step before a name becomes AOP. Only wine may still use the term **AOC**, if the producer wishes.

stops.name: IGP
stops.text: The wine’s quality or reputation is linked to where it’s from. For wine, every step from **harvest to finished wine** happens in the zone.

stops.name: Inside an AOP
stops.text: French appellations nest. In **Bordeaux**, a wine can be plain **Bordeaux AOC**, a sub-region like **Haut-Médoc**, or a commune like **Pauillac**. **Burgundy** climbs from **Regional** to **Village**, **Premier Cru** and **Grand Cru**.

read.visualIntro: AOP and IGP side by side:
read.mixup: **AOP** is the EU-wide name. **AOC** is France’s own step before it.

keyPoints.line: must have been a DOC for at least seven years.

read.bigIdea: Italy’s protected wines come in two tiers: DOCG and DOC.
read.where: Under Italian law, protected-origin (**DOP**) wines are either **DOCG** or **DOC**, and **IGT** is Italy’s word for IGP. A DOC zone must have been IGT for at least **five years**. A DOCG must have been a DOC for at least **seven years**, with stricter rules.

stops.name: Classico
stops.text: From the **oldest zone** of origin, like **Chianti Classico**.

stops.name: Riserva
stops.text: Extra aging: at least **two years** for reds and **one year** for whites.

stops.name: Superiore
stops.text: At least 10% lower yields and at least 0.5% more alcohol than the base wine.

stops.name: Gran Selezione
stops.text: Only for **DOCG** wines made from the estate’s **own grapes**.

read.mixup: **DOCG** sits above **DOC**: it needs seven years as a DOC and stricter rules.

keyPoints.line: needs prestige and five years as a quality region.
needs 10+ years as a DO and bottling in the zone.

read.bigIdea: Spain’s labels tell you where, and how long it aged.
read.where: Spanish law sets the place terms, from **Vino de la Tierra** (Spain’s IGP) up to **DOCa**. Aging words like **Crianza** and **Gran Reserva** tell you the minimum time the wine aged.

stops.name: Vino de la Tierra
stops.text: Spanish law uses this term for **IGP** wines.

stops.name: DO
stops.text: Needs **high prestige** and at least **five years** as a recognized quality region. **Cava** is a DO for traditional-method sparkling wine.

stops.name: DOCa
stops.text: Needs at least **10 years as a DO**, and the wine must be bottled by wineries inside the zone. **Rioja** and **Priorat** are DOCa.

stops.name: Vino de Pago
stops.text: A protected-origin wine from one named site (a **pago**) with its own soil and microclimate. All the grapes must grow there.

read.mixup: **Spanish law** and **Rioja** set different minimum times. For Level 1, just know the order: **Crianza**, **Reserva**, **Gran Reserva**.

read.bigIdea: German law grades wine by how ripe the grapes are.
read.where: The **1971 wine law** made ripeness at harvest the main measure of quality. **Qualitätswein** comes from one of **13 regions**. **Prädikatswein** is Qualitätswein graded by ripeness, and it may not be enriched (**chaptalized**). Those 13 regions are the **Anbaugebiete**.
read.stopsTitle: The six Prädikate, least to most ripe

stops.name: Kabinett and Spätlese
stops.text: Off-dry in style, and both can be made **trocken** (dry).

stops.name: Auslese
stops.text: The next step up in ripeness at harvest.

stops.name: Beerenauslese and Eiswein
stops.text: **Beerenauslese** is very sweet. **Eiswein** is just as ripe, but picked at **minus 7°C** or colder and pressed while frozen.

stops.name: Trockenbeerenauslese
stops.text: The top of the ladder, and very sweet.

read.visualIntro: Germany’s four tiers, top to bottom:
read.mixup: **Ripeness is not sweetness.** A Kabinett or Spätlese can be dry: the winemaker decides how sweet it ends up.
read.sayIt: Trocken on the label means this one is dry.

keyPoints.line: is Austria’s quality appellation, much like an AOC.
is the ripest level on the Wachau’s own ladder.
on the capsule marks Austrian quality wine.
is the word for protected wines in Portugal.
to know: Vinho Verde, Douro, Porto and Madeira.

read.bigIdea: Austria and Portugal have their own label words.
read.where: **Austria** uses tiers that look like Germany’s: **Wein**, **Landwein**, **Qualitätswein** and **Prädikatswein**. Its own addition is the **DAC**. **Portugal** calls its protected wines **DOP**.

stops.name: DAC
stops.text: **Districtus Austriae Controllatus.** A quality wine from a named area, like an **AOC** or **DOC**. Each DAC sets its grapes and styles, and the focus is on **dry** wines.

stops.name: Prädikatswein
stops.text: Graded by ripeness as in Germany, but **rarely made** in Austria. **Landwein**, the regional tier, is rarely exported.

stops.name: Smaragd
stops.text: The **Wachau** has its own system based on grape ripeness at harvest. **Smaragd**, named for the green lizards in the vines, is the ripest level.

stops.name: The capsule
stops.text: Austrian quality wine carries a **red-white-red** band on the capsule. The Court expects you to recognize it.

stops.name: DOP
stops.text: Portugal’s protected wines are **DOP**. Know four: **Vinho Verde** (low alcohol, a slight fizz), **Douro** (bold dry reds), **Porto** (fortified sweet red) and **Madeira** (fortified white, dry to sweet).

read.mixup: **Smaragd** is a Wachau ripeness level. **DAC** is a place-based appellation used across Austria.

keyPoints.line: is a US growing region with its own features and border.

read.bigIdea: US label rules come down to a few percentages.
read.where: An **AVA** (American Viticultural Area) is a defined growing region with a name, its own features and a set boundary. Showing a **vintage** or a **grape name** means the label must also show an appellation.

stops.name: Grape variety
stops.text: Name one grape and at least **75%** of the wine must be that grape. Name two or more and the label must show each percentage.

stops.name: State or county
stops.text: At least **75%** must come from the named state or county.

stops.name: AVA
stops.text: At least **85%** must come from grapes grown in the AVA.

stops.name: Vineyard or vintage
stops.text: A **vineyard name** needs **95%** from that vineyard. A **vintage** with an AVA needs **95%** from that year; with a state or county, **85%**.

stops.name: Oregon
stops.text: The Court lists Oregon at **90%** for most named grapes (with exceptions such as **Cabernet Sauvignon** and **Merlot**) and **95%** from a named AVA.

read.visualIntro: The federal minimums on one chart:
read.mixup: **Estate Bottled** has legal rules: an AVA, and grapes the winery owns or controls. **Reserve** has no legal meaning.

South Eastern Australia spans several states.

read.bigIdea: New World labels mostly promise where, not how.
read.where: Most New World place names promise **origin**, not a style. A Chilean **DO** or an Australian **GI** names where the grapes grew, with no other rules attached. The numbers to know are the **minimum percentages** behind a grape or place name.

stops.name: Chile
stops.text: The **Denominación de Origen** marks origin only. Places nest from **Region** to **Subregion**, **Zone** and **Area**.

stops.name: Argentina
stops.text: Name a grape and at least **85%** of the wine must be that grape.

stops.name: South Africa
stops.text: A wine from a single appellation must be **100%** from it, and certification is strict. The places, big to small: **Geographical Unit**, **Region**, **District** and **Ward**.

stops.name: Australia and New Zealand
stops.text: A **GI** names the origin. Both need **85%** of a named grape, and Australia’s 85% also covers **vintage** and **origin**. Australian GIs nest from **Australia** to **State**, **Zone**, **Region** and **Sub-Region**.

stops.name: Canada and Mexico
stops.text: Canada has **no national wine law**: each province sets its own, and **VQA** oversees premium wine. The Court’s guide says Mexico has **no wine laws** at all.

read.visualIntro: Big to small, three ways to nest a place:
read.mixup: **Australia** needs 85% of a named grape. The **United States** needs only 75%.

keyPoints.line: producer, region, grape or appellation, vintage, alcohol.
Then the appellation’s rules tell you what’s inside.
means non-vintage: it can blend wine from several years.

read.bigIdea: Every label answers who, where, what and when.
read.where: Look for five things: the producer, the region, the grape or appellation, the vintage, and the alcohol. If no grape is named, the **appellation’s rules** tell you what’s in the bottle. Producers design labels and capsules within each government’s **label laws**.

stops.name: NV
stops.text: No single year on the label. The wine can blend several **vintages**.

stops.name: Estate bottled
stops.text: **Mis en bouteille au château** or **au domaine** in France, **Imbottigliato all’origine** in Italy, **Erzeugerabfüllung** in Germany.

stops.name: Reserve and Old Vines
stops.text: **Reserve** has no official meaning, and **Old Vines** has no rule for how old the vines are.

stops.name: Burgundy words
stops.text: A **négociant** buys grapes or wine. A **clos** is a walled vineyard, and a **monopole** is a vineyard controlled by one winery. **Domaine** and **Vieilles Vignes** (old vines) are the other words the Court lists.
